subtopics.example: A health insurer replaces broad virtual private network (VPN) access with identity-aware access for claims staff. Kwame, a junior security analyst, sees a denied sign-in for a claims manager whose laptop failed its disk encryption check. Kwame confirms the policy worked as designed, explains the fix to the user and passes the laptop to desktop support, instead of granting an exception.

review: Inventory resources reachable without passing a gateway or agent
Compare denied requests with policy to confirm correct decisions
Track exceptions to see who approved them
evidence: Policy engine decision logs with reasons
Inventory of resources and their enforcement points
Exception register with approver and expiry date
audit_focus.recommend: Send exception requests to the policy owner and report unguarded resources to the security lead.
audit_focus.decides: The resource's policy owner approves or refuses a waiver

subtopics.isaca_rule: Deciding and enforcing are separate jobs: the decision point decides and the enforcement point acts. Every protected resource needs an enforcement point in front of it, and exceptions to a denied request go to the policy owner, not around the policy.

exam_traps.trap: The enforcement point decides who gets access.
exam_traps.why: The enforcement point only carries out the decision. The policy engine makes it, and the policy administrator passes it on.

exam_traps.trap: Zero Trust Network Access is just a faster VPN.
exam_traps.why: A typical VPN places the user on the network. Zero Trust Network Access connects a verified user and device to one application at a time and keeps checking during the session.

key_terms.definition: The policy engine and policy administrator together: the part that decides on access and signals the result.
The gateway or agent in front of a resource that allows, blocks or ends a session.
Remote access that connects a verified user and device to a single application rather than to the whole network.

subtopics.memory_aid: The engine decides, the administrator signals, the enforcement point acts.

subtopics.name: Network Access Control (NAC)
subtopics.definition: Network access control (NAC) checks who and what is connecting to a network, and whether the device meets security policy, before granting the right level of access.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Anyone can plug a laptop into a meeting-room port or join Wi-Fi with a shared password. NAC keeps unknown or unhealthy devices away from sensitive systems.
how_it_works: IEEE 802.1X gives port-based access: the device asks the switch or access point, which checks with an authentication server before opening the port.
Posture checks look at device health, such as patch level, antivirus status and disk encryption, before or after the device is admitted.
Devices that fail go to a quarantine network until fixed, and guests go to a guest network.
Devices that cannot run 802.1X, like printers and cameras, are identified by profiling and given limited access, not a free pass.
NAC supports Zero Trust by feeding device identity and health into access decisions.
subtopics.example: At a law firm, a visitor plugs a laptop into a conference-room network port. NAC finds no company certificate and places the laptop on the guest virtual LAN (VLAN) with internet-only access. Ravi, a junior network technician, sees the event, confirms it matches policy and notes it in the shift log, without moving the laptop onto the internal network for convenience.

review: Compare connected devices with the known-device list
Confirm failed devices land in the quarantine network
Identify ports or access points that bypass the check
evidence: NAC event logs showing admit, quarantine and deny decisions
Device profiles for printers and cameras
Switch settings showing which ports enforce 802.1X
audit_focus.recommend: Report bypassed ports and unknown devices to the network lead rather than admitting them manually.
audit_focus.decides: The policy owner approves any NAC exception

subtopics.isaca_rule: Admission should depend on verified identity and device health, not on finding a free port. Devices that fail checks go to remediation, and exceptions go to the policy owner. Convenience is not a reason to skip the check.

exam_traps.trap: Media access control (MAC) address filtering gives the same protection as NAC.
exam_traps.why: MAC addresses are easy to copy. NAC authenticates the user or device with credentials or certificates and can also check its health.

exam_traps.trap: Devices that fail a posture check should simply be blocked.
exam_traps.why: The usual design quarantines them with access only to updates and fixes, so they can be remediated and then admitted.

key_terms.definition: The device or software asking to join the network in an 802.1X exchange.
A protocol for central sign-in checks, often the server behind 802.1X.
Checking a device's security state, such as patches and antivirus, before or during access.
A restricted segment for devices that fail checks, allowing only remediation services.

subtopics.memory_aid: Who are you, what are you, are you healthy? Then you get in.

subtopics.name: Segmenting AI Development Environments
subtopics.definition: Segmenting artificial intelligence (AI) development environments means keeping model building, training and testing on separate, controlled network segments, away from production systems and their sensitive data.
subtopics.why_it_matters: AI work needs large datasets and broad tools, and experiments are less locked down than production. Without isolation, a weak notebook server or a careless copy can expose real customer data or a live model.
how_it_works: Development, training and production run on different segments, with firewall or policy rules between them.
Development uses masked, sampled or synthetic data; bringing in real sensitive data needs the data owner's approval.
Training data gets Zero Trust treatment: named access, healthy devices, least privilege and a log of every read.
Outbound traffic from AI environments is restricted, so data cannot be sent to unapproved external AI services or storage.
Trained models and their datasets are protected assets, because tampering with either can poison the model's behavior.
subtopics.example: A retail chain's data science team asks for a full copy of the loyalty-card database on its experiment servers, which share a segment with office laptops. Bao, a junior security analyst, notices those servers can also reach the internet freely. Bao takes the request to the data owner and the security lead, suggesting an isolated training segment and masked data.

review: Confirm AI environments sit on their own segment
Sample datasets on experiment servers for signed release forms
Confirm outbound traffic is limited to approved destinations
evidence: Firewall exports for the experiment and live environments
Data owner approvals for each dataset used
Egress logs from AI servers
audit_focus.recommend: Escalate real sensitive data or open internet access in AI environments to the data owner and security lead.
audit_focus.decides: The data owner decides which data AI teams may use

subtopics.isaca_rule: AI experiments belong in their own segment, using the least sensitive data that will do the job, with outbound traffic restricted. Real sensitive data enters only with the data owner's approval, and training data gets the same Zero Trust protection as any high-value asset.

exam_traps.trap: AI development servers are internal, so they can safely reach production data and the internet.
exam_traps.why: Internal does not mean trusted. Development environments are less hardened, so open links to production data and the internet create easy paths for leaks and poisoning.

exam_traps.trap: Isolation is unnecessary when the AI model will only be used internally.
exam_traps.why: The training data and the model are valuable whoever uses them. Leaked training data is a breach, and a poisoned model gives wrong answers internally too.

key_terms.definition: Artificially generated data that mimics the patterns of real data without containing real people's records.
A trained model file and its settings, protected from theft and tampering like source code.
Controlling outbound traffic so only approved destinations can be reached.

subtopics.memory_aid: Sandbox the experiment, mask the data, watch the exit.

topics.overview: This topic covers what makes a service a cloud service, the ways cloud is delivered and deployed, and how security duties split between the customer and the provider. It ends with the most common ways cloud data is exposed and with AI workloads hosted in the cloud.
can_do: Name the five essential characteristics of cloud computing and spot each one in a scenario
Match a scenario to IaaS, PaaS or SaaS, and to a public, private, community or hybrid cloud
Say who patches, configures and protects each layer under each service model
Recognize a cloud misconfiguration or AI data leak and route it to the right owner

subtopics.name: The Five Essential Characteristics of Cloud Computing
subtopics.definition: Cloud computing is using computing resources, such as servers, storage and software, from a shared pool over a network, taking more or less as needed and paying for use.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The five characteristics explain both the benefits and the risks. Self-service and elasticity speed things up, but they also let anyone with an account create, expose or delete resources in minutes.
how_it_works: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) SP 800-145 names five essential characteristics; a service lacking them is closer to traditional hosting.
Each characteristic brings a security duty: self-service needs strong account control, and pooling needs strong separation between customers.
Elastic resources appear and disappear quickly, so asset inventories and log collection must update automatically.
Broad network access means management consoles can be reached from anywhere, so they need multifactor authentication (MFA).
Metering shows who uses what, so unexpected cost spikes can also reveal misuse, such as hijacked accounts mining cryptocurrency.

types.meaning: Customers set up servers, storage or accounts themselves through a portal or API, without waiting for provider staff.
Services are reached over the network from many kinds of devices, such as laptops, phones and tablets.
The provider serves many customers from shared hardware, assigning resources as needed; customers rarely know the exact location.
Capacity grows or shrinks quickly, often automatically, to match demand, so it seems almost unlimited.
Use, such as storage or processing time, is metered, so it can be monitored, reported and billed.

subtopics.example: During a holiday sale, an online florist's website automatically adds servers as traffic grows, then removes them overnight. Afterward, Elena, a junior cloud support analyst, finds several temporary servers missing from the asset list, with their logs gone. Elena reports the gap to the cloud platform owner, so inventory and log collection run for every new server.

review: Sample recently created resources for tags, owner and logging
Confirm management console accounts use MFA
Compare usage and cost reports with expected levels
evidence: Resource listing from the provider console with tags
Console account list showing MFA status
Monthly usage and billing reports
audit_focus.recommend: Report untracked resources, accounts without MFA or unexplained cost spikes to the cloud platform owner.
audit_focus.decides: The cloud platform owner decides account and resource rules

subtopics.isaca_rule: Match the scenario's words to the characteristic: 'scales automatically' is rapid elasticity, 'pay for what you use' is measured service, 'shared hardware' is resource pooling, 'set it up yourself' is on-demand self-service, and 'from any device' is broad network access.

exam_traps.trap: Rapid elasticity and resource pooling mean the same thing.
exam_traps.why: Pooling is the provider sharing hardware among many customers. Elasticity is one customer's capacity growing and shrinking quickly with demand.

exam_traps.trap: Virtualization is one of the five essential characteristics.
exam_traps.why: Virtualization is a technology that makes pooling possible, not one of the five. They are self-service, broad network access, pooling, elasticity and measured service.

key_terms.definition: Many customers, or tenants, sharing the same provider infrastructure while kept logically separate.
A defined way for software to request services from other software; cloud resources are often created and changed through APIs.

subtopics.memory_aid: Self-serve, from anywhere, shared, stretchy, metered.

subtopics.name: Virtualization and Containers in the Cloud
subtopics.definition: Virtualization uses software called a hypervisor to run many isolated virtual machines on one physical server; containers share one operating system kernel but keep applications apart.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Cloud resource pooling depends on this isolation. If it breaks, one customer could reach another's data, and a badly built image can be copied into hundreds of running workloads.
how_it_works: A Type 1 hypervisor runs directly on the hardware, as in cloud data centers; a Type 2 hypervisor runs on an ordinary operating system, as on a laptop.
Each virtual machine has its own operating system; containers are lighter because they share the host's kernel, so their isolation is thinner.
Workloads start from images, so one hardened, patched image protects every copy, and one flawed image spreads the flaw everywhere.
Serverless computing runs small pieces of code on demand; the provider manages the servers, and the customer secures the code, permissions and data.
The provider secures the hypervisor and physical hosts; the customer secures what runs inside, as the service model sets.
subtopics.example: A startup builds every web server from one container image downloaded from a public registry. Tariq, a junior DevOps engineer, scans the image and finds an outdated library with a known critical flaw. Because every running container came from that image, Tariq reports the finding to the platform lead and asks for a patched, approved base image as the team standard.

review: Trace running containers back to their source registry
Compare image contents with known vulnerability reports
Identify serverless functions with broad permissions
evidence: Vulnerability findings for each stored template
Approved base image list with patch dates
Permission settings attached to each serverless function
audit_focus.recommend: Report flawed images or over-privileged functions to the platform lead and request an approved replacement.
audit_focus.decides: The platform owner approves base images and permissions

subtopics.isaca_rule: Secure the template, not just the copy: harden and patch images, and pull them only from approved sources. The provider owns hypervisor isolation; the customer owns whatever it places inside the virtual machine, container or function.

exam_traps.trap: Containers are as isolated from each other as virtual machines are.
exam_traps.why: Containers share the host's kernel, so one kernel flaw can affect all of them. Virtual machines each run their own operating system, which gives stronger separation.

exam_traps.trap: Serverless means the customer has nothing left to secure.
exam_traps.why: The provider runs the servers, but the customer still owns the function's code, its permissions, its secrets and the data it handles.

key_terms.definition: Software that creates and runs virtual machines and keeps them separated on shared hardware.
An attack that breaks out of a virtual machine to reach the hypervisor or other virtual machines.
A saved template from which virtual machines or containers are started.

subtopics.memory_aid: VMs bring their own operating system; containers share one; serverless hides it.

subtopics.name: Cloud Service Models: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS
subtopics.definition: Cloud service models describe what the provider delivers: infrastructure as a service (IaaS), platform as a service (PaaS) for running code, or software as a service (SaaS).
subtopics.why_it_matters: The service model decides how much the customer must manage and secure. Misreading it leaves layers that nobody patches or protects.
how_it_works: IaaS rents out virtual servers, storage and networks; the customer installs and manages the operating system and everything above it.
PaaS offers a managed runtime, database or development platform; the customer brings and secures the application code and its settings.
SaaS delivers a complete application over the internet; the customer manages users, settings and the data it puts in.
Moving from IaaS toward SaaS hands more layers to the provider, but the customer gives up control and visibility in return.
Specialist offerings, such as database or artificial intelligence services, usually behave like PaaS or SaaS when deciding who secures what.

rows.label: Provider delivers
cells: A managed platform for running code

rows.label: Customer manages
cells: Operating system, middleware, apps, data, access

rows.label: Example use
cells: Renting virtual machines to host an older business app
Deploying a web app without managing servers
Using online email or a payroll service

subtopics.example: A city council moves staff email to a SaaS email service. Weeks later, Pedro, a junior IT analyst, finds that file sharing is set to 'anyone with the link' by default. Pedro knows the provider runs the service but the council configures it. Pedro reports the setting to the service owner, who approves a change to internal-only sharing.

review: Identify the service model for each cloud service in use
Confirm customer-side settings follow the security baseline
List the layers the organization must patch for each service
evidence: Cloud service inventory labeled IaaS, PaaS or SaaS
SaaS sharing and access settings
Patch records for customer-managed layers
audit_focus.recommend: Raise risky sharing or access settings with the service owner and apply only approved changes.
audit_focus.decides: The service owner decides the configuration of each cloud service

subtopics.isaca_rule: Ask what the customer still controls. In IaaS, that is nearly everything above the hardware; in PaaS, the code and its settings; in SaaS, users, configuration and data. In every model, the customer owns its data and decides who can reach it.

exam_traps.trap: With SaaS, the provider is responsible for everything, including who can see the data.
exam_traps.why: The provider runs the application, but the customer decides who has accounts, what they can reach and how sharing is set. Those settings cause many SaaS data leaks.

exam_traps.trap: PaaS customers must patch the operating system under their application.
exam_traps.why: In PaaS, the provider patches the operating system and runtime. The customer secures its own code, the libraries it adds, its configuration and its data.

key_terms.definition: Software between the operating system and applications, such as web servers, runtimes and message queues.
A general label for services delivered from the cloud, such as database or security as a service.

subtopics.memory_aid: IaaS: rent the kitchen. PaaS: use a staffed kitchen. SaaS: order the meal.

subtopics.name: Cloud Deployment Models
subtopics.definition: Cloud deployment models describe who the cloud infrastructure is built for and shared with: public, private, community or hybrid.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The deployment model shapes control, cost and risk. Sensitive or regulated data may need more control than a public cloud gives by default, and every model added means more settings to secure.
how_it_works: A public cloud is open to any customer and owned by a provider; tenants share infrastructure but are kept logically apart.
A private cloud serves one organization only, on its own site or run by a provider, giving more control at higher cost.
A community cloud is shared by organizations with common needs, such as agencies or hospitals under the same rules.
A hybrid cloud joins two or more models, such as private for sensitive records and public for busy periods, with links that must be secured.
Using several public cloud providers is called multi-cloud; it reduces reliance on one provider but multiplies the settings to secure.

rows.label: Cost
cells: Pay per use, low starting cost

subtopics.example: Three regional hospitals plan to share a cloud platform built around their common health-privacy rules, run by one provider and closed to everyone else. Yusuf, a junior security analyst at one hospital, is asked which model this is. Yusuf identifies a community cloud and points out that the hospitals must agree in writing who manages access and security.

review: Identify the deployment model of each cloud service
Confirm links between private and public parts are secured
Compare where data is stored with legal location rules
evidence: Cloud service inventory with deployment model
Agreements naming who manages access in shared clouds
Data location settings in each service
audit_focus.recommend: Report data stored outside permitted locations, or unsecured hybrid links, to the cloud owner and legal team.
audit_focus.decides: Management and legal counsel decide where regulated data may live

subtopics.isaca_rule: Identify the model by who shares the infrastructure: anyone (public), one organization (private), a group with common needs (community) or a combination (hybrid). Wherever it runs, the organization keeps responsibility for its own data and access.

exam_traps.trap: A private cloud has to be in the organization's own building.
exam_traps.why: Private means used by one organization only. A provider can host and run it off site; location does not define it.

exam_traps.trap: Hybrid cloud and multi-cloud mean the same thing.
exam_traps.why: Hybrid combines different deployment models, such as private and public. Multi-cloud uses several providers, which may all be public.

key_terms.definition: The principle that data is subject to the laws of the country where it is stored or processed.
Moving extra workload from a private cloud to a public cloud when demand spikes.

subtopics.memory_aid: Public: anyone. Private: one. Community: a club. Hybrid: a mix.

subtopics.name: The Shared Responsibility Model
subtopics.definition: The shared responsibility model divides cloud security duties between provider and customer: the provider secures the cloud itself, and the customer secures what it puts in the cloud.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Many cloud breaches come from customers assuming the provider handles something it does not, such as access settings. Knowing the split for each service model shows who must patch, configure and monitor each layer.
how_it_works: The provider always secures the physical data centers, the hardware, and the core network and virtualization that run the service.
The customer always owns its data, its user accounts and access rights, its own devices and how it configures the service.
In IaaS, the customer also patches the guest operating system, middleware and applications.
In PaaS, the provider patches the operating system and runtime; the customer secures the application code and settings.
In SaaS, the provider runs and patches the application; the customer manages users, access, sharing settings and data.
The contract and the provider's documentation set the exact split, which can differ from one service to another.

rows.label: Application
cells: Provider runs it; customer sets its configuration

Confirm customer-owned layers have patch and configuration owners
Identify tasks each party assumes the other does

subtopics.isaca_rule: The provider owns security of the cloud; the customer owns security in the cloud. Data, identities, access and configuration stay with the customer in every model. The closer to SaaS, the more the provider patches.

exam_traps.trap: Moving to the cloud transfers accountability for a data breach to the provider.
exam_traps.why: The customer stays accountable for its data and who can reach it in every model. Contracts can share duties, but accountability for the data stays with its owner.

exam_traps.trap: In IaaS, the provider patches the operating systems of the customer's virtual machines.
exam_traps.why: In IaaS, the provider secures the hardware and hypervisor. The guest operating system and everything installed on it are the customer's to patch.

key_terms.definition: Remaining answerable for an outcome even when someone else does the work.
A table, often from the provider, showing which party handles each security task for each service.

subtopics.memory_aid: Provider: security of the cloud. Customer: security in the cloud.

subtopics.name: Cloud Roles and Agreements
subtopics.definition: Cloud roles name the parties involved in a cloud service, such as customer, provider, broker, carrier and auditor, and agreements set out what each party must do.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Shared duties work only when written down and checked. A customer who never reads the agreement or the provider's assurance reports cannot know which risks are still its own.
how_it_works: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) SP 500-292 names five actors, listed below; one organization can play several.
The service level agreement sets measurable promises, such as availability and support response times, and the remedy when they are missed.
Contracts should cover data location, breach notification, data return and deletion at exit, and evidence about controls.
Providers show their controls through independent reports and certifications, such as SOC 2 reports and ISO/IEC 27001 certificates.
Inside the customer, owners are still named: the data owner, the system owner and the team that runs cloud accounts.

types.meaning: The organization or person that uses the cloud service and owns its data and accounts.
The organization that runs the cloud infrastructure and makes the service available.
A go-between that combines, manages or adds value to services from several providers.
The network or telecom provider that carries traffic between consumers and providers.
An independent party that assesses cloud services and controls and reports on them.

subtopics.example: A small accounting firm is choosing a SaaS document service. Rosa, a junior IT coordinator, is asked to gather security information. Rosa requests the provider's latest independent security report and its service level agreement, notes that the contract says nothing about deleting data at exit, and passes the findings to the managing partner, who decides whether to sign.

review: Read the draft agreement against a checklist of required clauses
Compare the provider's assurance report scope with the services used
Confirm the assurance report is current
evidence: Draft contract with its uptime and support commitments
Third-party attestation covering the period and services in use
Written plan for leaving the provider and retrieving records
audit_focus.recommend: Pass contract gaps and outdated assurance reports to the business owner before signing or renewal.
audit_focus.decides: The business owner who signs decides whether to accept gaps

subtopics.isaca_rule: Get it in writing and get evidence. Before a cloud service goes live, the agreement should say who does what, and independent reports should show the provider does its part. Gaps go to the business owner who signs.

exam_traps.trap: A provider's ISO/IEC 27001 certificate means the customer has no security work left.
exam_traps.why: The certificate covers the provider's own controls in its stated scope, not the customer's configuration, accounts or data handling.

exam_traps.trap: The service level agreement guarantees the service will not go down.
exam_traps.why: An SLA sets a target, such as 99.9% availability, and a remedy such as service credits. It does not prevent outages; the customer still plans for them.

key_terms.definition: A contract section setting measurable service targets and the remedies when they are missed.
An independent auditor's report on a service organization's controls for security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality or privacy.
A contract clause letting the customer, or an auditor it chooses, assess the provider's controls.

subtopics.memory_aid: Write it down, then prove it.

subtopics.name: Protecting Data in the Cloud
subtopics.definition: Protecting cloud data means classifying it, encrypting it in transit and at rest, deciding who controls the keys, and making sure it can be recovered and fully deleted.
subtopics.why_it_matters: In every service model, the data stays the customer's responsibility. Strong encryption with well-controlled keys limits the damage if storage is exposed or the provider is breached.
how_it_works: Classify data before it moves, so the most sensitive data gets the strongest controls or stays out of the cloud.
Encrypt data in transit with Transport Layer Security (TLS), and at rest with the provider's encryption service or the customer's own tools.
Keys may be managed by the provider, by the customer inside the provider's key service, or held by the customer entirely outside it.
Back up important cloud data, SaaS data included, because many services cannot restore deleted or ransomed files beyond a short window.
At exit, customers cannot wipe the provider's disks, so they delete their data and destroy its encryption keys.

rows.label: Who controls the keys
cells: The customer, inside the provider's key service

rows.label: If the customer loses the keys
cells: Not an issue; the provider holds them

subtopics.example: A marketing agency keeps client files in a SaaS file-sharing service. A staff account is compromised and ransomware encrypts the shared folders. The provider can restore only the last 30 days of file versions. Sofia, a junior IT technician, reports the incident to the incident lead and records that the agency had no separate backup, so the gap goes to the service owner.

review: Confirm sensitive cloud data is encrypted at rest and in transit
Identify who controls each encryption key
Confirm restores from independent backups have been tested
evidence: Encryption settings for storage and databases
Key service records of key owners and rotation
Backup restore test results for cloud data
audit_focus.recommend: Report unencrypted sensitive data or missing backups to the data owner and the service owner.
audit_focus.decides: The data owner decides classification and key control

subtopics.isaca_rule: The data is the customer's job in every model. Classify it, encrypt it, decide who holds the keys, keep independent backups of what matters and plan deletion at exit. If the customer loses keys it alone holds, the data is gone.

exam_traps.trap: Data encrypted by the provider is safe from any provider access.
exam_traps.why: If the provider manages the keys, it can technically decrypt the data. Customer-controlled keys reduce that exposure, at the cost of more work and more risk if keys are lost.

exam_traps.trap: Deleting a cloud file is enough to sanitize the data.
exam_traps.why: Copies can remain in backups and replicas the customer cannot reach. Destroying the encryption keys makes every remaining copy unreadable.

key_terms.definition: Making data unreadable by securely destroying the keys that encrypt it.
A cloud service that creates, stores, rotates and controls the use of encryption keys.
Where data is physically stored, often required by law or contract.

subtopics.memory_aid: Own the data, own the keys, own the backup.

subtopics.name: Cloud Misconfiguration, CSPM and CASB
subtopics.definition: A cloud misconfiguration is a setting that leaves resources more exposed than intended, such as public storage, open ports or excessive permissions; posture and broker tools help find it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Misconfiguration is among the most common causes of cloud data exposure, because self-service lets anyone create resources quickly. One wrong setting can publish millions of records.
how_it_works: Common mistakes include public storage, management ports open to the whole internet, unused accounts with broad rights, logging turned off and secret keys stored in code.
Secure baselines, such as the Center for Internet Security (CIS) Benchmarks for cloud platforms, describe what good settings look like.
Cloud security posture management (CSPM) tools scan accounts continuously, compare settings to the baseline and flag drift.
A cloud access security broker (CASB) sits between users and cloud services, showing which services are in use and enforcing data and access policy.
Infrastructure written as code can be reviewed and tested, catching mistakes before they go live.

rows.label: Looks at
cells: The organization's own cloud account settings
How users use cloud services, including unapproved ones

rows.label: Finds
cells: Public storage, open ports, weak settings
Shadow IT, risky sharing, data moving to unapproved apps

rows.label: Typical action
cells: Alert, or fix the setting back to the baseline
Block, warn or apply data protection rules

subtopics.example: A university research group creates a cloud storage bucket to share survey files with a partner and makes it public for convenience. The university's CSPM tool flags it within an hour. Wen, a junior cloud security analyst, confirms the bucket holds student names, notifies the bucket owner and the security lead under the incident procedure, and records when the exposure began.

review: Review open findings older than the agreed fix time
Confirm flagged findings are fixed or formally accepted
Identify unapproved cloud apps from broker reports
evidence: CSPM findings with dates found and fixed
Broker discovery report of unsanctioned apps
Cloud activity logs showing who changed a setting
audit_focus.recommend: Send baseline failures to the resource owner to fix, and escalate any exposed sensitive data as an incident.
audit_focus.decides: The resource owner fixes it or management accepts the risk

subtopics.isaca_rule: In the cloud, the likeliest breach is the customer's own setting, not the provider being hacked. Use baselines and continuous checks, and when a tool flags exposure, confirm what data is involved and report to the owner fast, because exposure time matters.

exam_traps.trap: If a cloud storage bucket was public, the provider caused the breach.
exam_traps.why: Storage permissions are a customer setting in every service model. The provider supplies the controls; the customer chooses how to set them.

exam_traps.trap: A CASB does the same job as a network firewall.
exam_traps.why: A firewall filters traffic by network rules. A CASB understands cloud services, users and data, so it can spot shadow IT and apply policy to one app or file.

key_terms.definition: Technology, such as cloud apps, that staff use without IT's knowledge or approval.
Gradual change of settings away from the approved baseline.
Defining servers, networks and settings in files that are reviewed and deployed automatically, like software.

subtopics.memory_aid: Check settings before attackers do: baseline, scan, fix, report.

subtopics.name: Shared Responsibility for AI Workloads
subtopics.definition: Shared responsibility for cloud-hosted artificial intelligence (AI) workloads splits security duties: the provider secures the AI platform; the customer secures data, prompts, access and use.
subtopics.why_it_matters: AI services make it easy to paste sensitive data into an outside model. Without knowing what the provider protects and what the terms allow, data can leak or be reused for training.
how_it_works: Before use, check the terms: whether prompts, the text and files users send, are stored, for how long, and whether they train the provider's models.
Allow only approved AI services, apply data classification rules to prompts, and use data loss prevention to stop sensitive data leaving.
Fine-tuned models and training data are customer assets, so they need access control, encryption and logging.
The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) report AI 100-2 E2025 and the OWASP Top 10 for large language model (LLM) applications describe attacks such as prompt injection.

subtopics.example: A clinic's billing team starts pasting patient invoices into a free public AI chatbot to draft payment letters. Marco, a junior IT security analyst, spots the traffic in web filter logs and finds the tool's terms allow prompts to be used for training. Marco reports it to the privacy officer and the security lead, who decide on an approved alternative.

audit_focus.recommend: Escalate AI tools without approved data-use terms to the security lead for review before wider use.
audit_focus.decides: Each data set's owner sets what may leave for outside models

subtopics.isaca_rule: An AI service is still a cloud service: the provider secures the platform; the customer owns data, prompts, access and settings. Use approved tools, check data-use terms first, and report sensitive data sent to unapproved AI services to the data owner or privacy lead.

exam_traps.trap: A well-known AI provider is responsible for protecting whatever data staff paste into it.
exam_traps.why: The customer decides what goes in. If the terms allow storage or training, pasted data has left the organization's control, however strong the provider's own security is.

exam_traps.trap: Blocking one public chatbot solves the AI data leakage risk.
exam_traps.why: Staff can reach many other AI services. Approved tools, training, data classification and data loss prevention cover the risk better.

key_terms.definition: Further training a ready-made model on an organization's own data, making the tuned model a sensitive asset.
Tools and rules that detect and stop sensitive data leaving through email, uploads or other channels.
Crafted or hidden instructions in input that make an AI model ignore its rules or reveal data.

key_terminologies.OSI model: A seven-layer reference model that splits network communication into separate jobs, from physical signals to applications.
key_terminologies.TCP/IP model: The four-layer model the internet runs on: Link, Internet, Transport and Application.
key_terminologies.MAC address: A hardware identifier used to deliver frames within one local network; easy to change in software.
key_terminologies.IP address: A logical address that routers use to move packets between networks; IPv4 is 32-bit and IPv6 is 128-bit.
key_terminologies.Port: A number from 0 to 65535 that tells a host which service should receive traffic.
key_terminologies.TCP: A connection-based transport protocol that delivers data reliably and in order.
key_terminologies.UDP: A connectionless transport protocol that is fast but does not guarantee delivery.
key_terminologies.TLS: Transport Layer Security: encrypts and authenticates connections such as HTTPS.
key_terminologies.SSH: Secure Shell: an encrypted protocol for remote command-line access and file transfer, replacing Telnet.
key_terminologies.VPN: Virtual private network: an encrypted tunnel across an untrusted network.
key_terminologies.Firewall: A device or software that allows or blocks traffic between networks or hosts by rules.
key_terminologies.IDS: Intrusion detection system: watches traffic or hosts and alerts on suspicious activity.
key_terminologies.IPS: Intrusion prevention system: sits in the traffic path and can block suspicious activity.
key_terminologies.WPA3: The current Wi-Fi security standard, using SAE sign-in and required management frame protection.
key_terminologies.Industrial control system (ICS): Embedded and networked computers that run physical processes such as power, water and manufacturing.
key_terminologies.Internet of Things (IoT): Everyday network-connected devices, such as cameras and sensors, that collect data or act with little human input.
key_terminologies.Network segmentation: Dividing a network into parts with controlled traffic between them.
key_terminologies.Screened subnet (DMZ): A zone for public-facing servers between the internet and internal networks.
key_terminologies.VLAN: Virtual local area network: a logical network carved out of a shared physical switch network.
key_terminologies.Micro-segmentation: Security policy applied to individual workloads, limiting each to the connections it needs.
key_terminologies.Defense in depth: Layering independent physical, technical and administrative controls so one failure does not expose the asset.
key_terminologies.Zero Trust: An approach that grants no trust based on network location and checks every request to every resource.
key_terminologies.Network access control (NAC): Checking a connecting user and device, and the device's health, before granting network access.
key_terminologies.Cloud computing: Using computing resources from a shared pool over a network, taking more or less as needed.
key_terminologies.IaaS, PaaS, SaaS: Cloud service models: rented infrastructure, a managed platform for code, or a finished application.
key_terminologies.Public, private, community, hybrid cloud: Cloud deployment models, defined by who the infrastructure is built for and shared with.
key_terminologies.Shared responsibility model: The split of cloud security duties: the provider secures the cloud, the customer secures what it puts in it.
key_terminologies.CASB: Cloud access security broker: sits between users and cloud services to show use and enforce policy.
key_terminologies.CSPM: Cloud security posture management: continuously checks cloud settings against a secure baseline.
